Southern District Health Board—Replacement of Board

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from Dr David Clark seeking to debate
under Standing Order 389 the dismissal of all members of the Southern District Health
Board and the appointment of a commissioner. This is a particular case of recent
occurrence involving ministerial responsibility. The dismissal of the board and the
appointment of a commissioner were announced this morning. This is an important
issue upon which debates have been held in the past. However, the Minister of Health
has made a mini sterial statement on the matter in the House today and, importantly, Dr
Clark has had the opportunity to comment on it. On this basis, I am not convinced that I
should set aside further business of the House today. The application is therefore
declined.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I move, That the House take note
of miscellaneous business . It all started so well. The freshly elected Government came
in. Bill English wen t to John Key and said: “We’ve got to do something. We’ve got to
do something for the poor, the indigent, and the hard up, for whom we’ve done nothing
for so long.” So he turned up here and said: “What about relief of poverty? Yep, we’ll
do that. What about the poor people at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment, who need a big screen and a new reception desk?”. That was ticked off as
well. “What about trade deals for the Middle East? We’ve got one little farm in the
middle of the desert with  no sheep on it. Yeah, we’ll tick that off as well.” And then
they came to housing —then they came to housing —because they have run the housing
stock down and they have got people living in poor -quality housing. Bill English said:
“Please, we’ve got to do s omething about housing.” Prime Minister John Key, because
17 Jun 2015 General Debate 4489
he does not like to think little, said: “Yep, we’ll go big on housing. We won’t have one
Minister; we’ll have three Ministers, and half a dozen associates if we have to have
them. And we will make housing the centrepiece of our Government for the foreseeable
future.” Then they appointed Nick Smith to run the programme, and that is where it all
started to unravel.
That is where it started to unravel because Nick Smith was left in charge of the most
pressing housing issues: out -of-control Auckland house prices, poor -quality rentals—a
whole range of things. He was given the job of fixing it all up. And so he started. He
had ignored the problem for several months to begin with. Pressed repeatedly by
members of the Opposition about what he was doing about out -of-control house prices,
he said: “What crisis of Auckland house prices? There isn’t one. What is the matter with
them?”. “Somebody can afford the houses.”, he said. “Somebody can afford expensive
houses. Oh, they’re all affordable.”, he said. Then he was pressed into actually having to
do something. Desperation turned to panic, and he has not stopped panicking since, so
that is where he is stuck now. He signed up councils for special housing areas —it was a
couple of years ago that the Government did that. Thousands of houses were promised.
The Prime Minister said yesterday that 8,500 houses had been built, and then he found
the truth: it was 170 houses. Two years on, and there are 170 houses for a cit y that
needs 20,000 houses a year just to catch up. So those members got that wrong as well.

items.speaker: Then those members said
items.text: “Oh, we will sort out the out -of-control house prices.
We’ll introduce a brightline test for the people who are buying more than one hous e.
We’ll make it for 2 years.” And so what did the property speculators all say? “Don’t
worry, we’ll sell them after 2 years.”, so that is not going to work. Then they said: “OK,
we accept that non-resident foreign buyers are a problem, so we’ll give them a couple of
hurdles to leap, and that will get them out of the market.” But the two hurdles were non-
resident foreign buyers having a bank account in New Zealand and an IRD number.
They can get them online just about. That is no hurdle at all. Then those m embers got to
the serious end of the business —the serious end of the business. They accepted finally
that they had to build more houses more quickly —housing supply. And they were not
just any houses; they had to be affordable —let us give them that. They un derstood that
they had to build affordable housing. So Nick Smith stumbled on the idea of a State -led
house-building programme, and he has not stopped stumbling since. He has not stopped
stumbling since.
Unfortunately, a whole number of missteps and mishaps occurred to this “Minister of
Outstanding Achievements”. It did not help that the plan was leaked. But leaks happen;
we all know that. Then those members announced that there were 500 hectares.
Remember? “Five hundred hectares —we’ve got land to burn. We’ re going to build
houses like you haven’t seen before.” Then they discovered that some of that land had
power substations on it and that some had cemeteries. One area of land was earmarked
for a motorway on-ramp. They cannot build on that one, so that was ditched. Then Nick

items.speaker: Smith said
items.text: “Right, I’ve got the journalists. They’re interested. I’ve got ’em on my side.
We’ll take ’em on the bus. We’ll ram a filled roll down their throats and say we’ve fed
them, and we’ll show them the land.” So he showed them 30 hectares —30 hectares of
land. Then it turned out that it was not his land to trade away. The local iwi had rights
over the land, so that plan then turned to custard as well. Then he denied that the iwi
had any rights at all. He told the Prime Minister “No,  Prime Minister, they have no
rights at all.” at the same time that he was going around saying to the iwi “We’ll give
you right of first refusal.”
What sort of Minister is this? What sort of Minister is this? So they had to concede:
“Listen, it was all ju st a guesstimate. It is all just a concept plan. We are not really sure
what we are doing. We do not know which way it is going to go.” But he does have one
4490 General Debate 17 Jun 2015
redeeming quality, Nick Smith. He is a man of great foresight. Seeing his fate as a
Minister, he re cently went bush with Maurice Williamson and started playing like a
possum and like road kill. Here he is in this photo, in his natural habitat. Road kill: that
is our Minister of Building and Housing.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The first line in that
speech was “It all started so well”, and in the end that is the line that is going to sum up
Andrew Little’s leadership, because that was a pathetic speech. If you are a Labour
supporter out there, watching on TV, you will be deeply disappointed. That man is the
leader of the Labour Party and in no way was that a Labour Party leader’s speech, and
those guys over there know it.
You know, there is a lot going on today. There is some big stuff, but what is Labour
focusing on? The minutiae —the stuff that nobody cares about. OK, housing is very
important. No question about that. Do not forget that Andrew Little is opposed to a
capital gains tax. So what does t hat mean for Labour’s caucus? Do you think David
Parker and David Cunliffe are going to fall in behind him? Frankly, on policy those
guys opposite are now absolutely fractured.
I am very disappointed that on a day that is incredibly important to the peopl e of
Otago and Southland, when we have put in a commissioner to turn round a dire
financial situation, the Labour leader does not have the quickness of mind, the
quickness on his feet, or the intellectual flexibility to deliver a speech that would make
some real difference to people in that region. Well, I can tell you: on health, that is a
battleground that Labour is no longer prepared to fight, because it has lost on health.
We have got a situation in the Southern District Health Board of worsening defic its
over many years. The financial forecasting has gone out the window. I could not rely on
those figures any longer. After a very considered period I took the step to announce
today that we are installing a commissioner, supported by two deputy commission ers,
into the Southern District Health Board. Why that is important is that the people of
Otago and Southland deserve high -quality health services, and, actually, until we can
have confidence in the finances, we can have no confidence that those services w ill be
delivered in the long term. We are totally committed to rebuilding Dunedin Hospital,
but it is very important that we have the governance arrangements that can implement
the strategic plan that is laid out. We need to know, actually, what the config uration of
services will be, before we can build the hospital. But that hospital absolutely will be
built, under National.
In terms of Otago and Southland—the southern region—we have put in an extra
$135 million over 7 years, and many, many more doctors and nurses. The definition of a
deficit is not underfunding; it is all about sensibly using the money that you are given.
So what I say to those members there is that, actually, $800 million -  plus for Otago -
Southland—for the Southern District Health Board—is a lot of money. We are now
relying on the commissioner, whom I have a great deal of faith in, to reconfigure those
services to deliver positively for the people of Otago and Southland.
I am really disappointed when you look at what Labour is focusing on. Clare Curran,
the MP for Dunedin South—do you know what she has had on her Twitter feed since it
became knowledge that we were going to announce a commissioner? Well, there have
been seven attacks on the Australian Government, three tweets in favour of Edward
Snowden, and only one tweet, retweeted from Annette King, about the Southern District
Health Board—and the Southern District Health Board is a big issue.
I am glad that we have support across the House for installing a commissioner. I
know it is very tempting for everyone to play politics with that. I know that that is going
to prove irresistible for some, but people like the MP for Dunedin North need to get
behind the commissioner or get out of the way. Actually Opposition MPs can be a very
17 Jun 2015 General Debate 4491
constructive part of the solution down there, and it is going to be very important that we
support Kathy Grant, Richard Thomson, and Graham Crombie as the commissioning
team.
We are not being political about this. Richard Thomson, a well -known Labour Party
member, and previously chair of the district health board down there —I do not care. He
is the right guy to put in there for the job. We have got the best people there to turn
round the health services and the finances, for the people of the Southern District Health
Board. This is a very considered decision we have made today, but it had to be made. I
think the future will be good, given that the commissioner has a big task in front of her.
Thank you.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: So soon this has become a
smug, arrogant Government, prepared to covertly lean on the media because it cannot
stand the heat. It is very clear that the Māori Party decided to ring up Māori Televis ion
because members did not want to front with a New Zealand First person on the panel.
The reason is, of course, that we know what they are up to, and we said from the word
“go” that they were not going to be a success. Although they might have sucked the
National members into it, they are going to fall with them as well.
There is also a story up in the North, and what the story says is that there is gold in
those wetlands of Northland. How did the Hon Judith Collins describe the place where
swamp kauri comes from? “I don’t like wetlands—they’re swamps.”, she exclaimed, on
TV3 last year. “I don’t like wetlands —they’re swamps.” No doubt, there are a few on
the backbenches of National wondering what this has got to do with Judith Collins. If
you were talking  about Oravida Kauri, they would more likely answer: “We like
wetlands—they’re goldmines.” The unlawful mining of swamp kauri is a practice that is
robbing Northland and robbing New Zealand, but robbing is a trait that this Government
has perfected into an  art form, while the same officials who run “honesty box”
biosecurity allow precious ancient timber to be exported whilst almost zero added value
occurs for Northland and for New Zealand. Plus there is the environmental despoliation
in so many cases.
This is incompetence built upon a rort that must stop, and New Zealand First calls
upon the Government to stop turning a blind eye and start enforcing the law that we
already have and that is capable of doing the job, if the Minister but did his job. This is
like the Wild West, and it is no wonder. In 2012 the Northern Advocate , which is the
paper at Whangarei, wrote that if swamp kauri averaged $71.66 a superfoot in old
money, ancient swamp kauri the size of Tane Mahuta would be worth $7 million—just
the one.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: How much?

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Seven million dollars. In 2012 the manager of
Oravida—it keeps on coming back, does it not? It will never go away. I mean, you can
be in the women’s magazine. You can be putting yourself out there, in a rather trashy,
American way. It is the kind of distinguished thing that New Zealand First would never
sink to: going in the magazines and holding your private life out there because she is on
a mission to get back. But I am telling  those colleagues over there that there is more.
Anyway, the manager of Oravida Kauri’s Ruakākā yard confirmed that by the end of
2012 it would have 2,800 tonnes of swamp kauri harvested. In today’s dollars that is
$71 million.
This is serious money, bree ding serious illegality, because in law swamp kauri must
be turned into a finished item before it is exported.

items.speaker: Alfred Ngaro
items.text: All the drama.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Now, there is no use in Alfred Ngaro— who should
understand these things, who should understand the cultural significance of what I am
4492 General Debate 17 Jun 2015
talking about, let alone the environmental matters —thinking it is a drama. It is a drama,
all right. It will be a real dr ama by the time we are finished. This is serious money,
breeding serious illegality, because in law swamp kauri must be turned into a finished
item before it is exported. The Forests Act 1949 defines “finished” as being a
manufactured wood product in its f inal state that is ready to be installed or used for its
intended purpose. We are talking furniture, picture frames, and, yes, even carvings. It is
important to understand, and the people of Northland know this, that dressed or rough -
sawn timber is not —I repeat, not—a finished or manufactured product. So how can the
Minister for Primary Industries, the Minister of Conservation, and the Minister for
Māori Development class a raw log with shallow chiselled Māori carvings or titivated
surface decorations as a finished product? The Minister for Primary Industries got up in
the House today, and he is out there talking to the media right now. The fact that a
kaumātua blessed some of these logs is totally irrelevant. There is always a kaumātua
for sale if the price is right. Members opposite would not know what a kaumātua was if
they fell over one. The one log cleared by both the Ministry for Primary Industries and
AsureQuality as being a finished carving got the export tick to go to Fuzhou Yima
Trading Company in C hina. In short, to conclude, there is an almighty rort going on
with private products, right under the Government’s nose, but because it has Chinese
friends and a former Minister’s husband who are involved, it will not raise a finger.
Well, we are going to raise the roof.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: One of the more
challenging aspects of delivering better public services for New Zealand is that fro m
time to time Governments need to make really tough decisions, and today has been one
of those days. I want to applaud Dr Coleman, our Minister of Health, for the difficult
decision that he has made to appoint commissioners to the Southern District Health
Board, an organisation that I know very well having worked there, albeit it quite some
time ago. I want to start my intervention by applauding those many thousands of hard-
working staff of the Southern District Health Board, the regional hospitals, and the
contractors to the delivery of health services in the south because they do a fantastic job
for our people, but there is a problem. There is a problem of financial viability that, as
the Minister said, is very longstanding. During the period from my last  year at Dunedin
Hospital, in 1996, until my first year as a member of Parliament, the combined deficits
of the Otago District Health Board were around $144 million. That sounds quite
challenging in and of itself, but the budgeted deficits during that peri od were only half
that. What has frustrated successive Ministers on both sides of the House is that
successive returns to viability plans have been tabled and not adhered to. So what is
really important now is that there be a circuit breaker, and I think t hat is what the
appointment of commissioners will do.
I was very pleased, albeit not surprised, to note the Minister of Health’s commitment
to the rebuilding of the clinical services block and the hospital in the foreseeable future.
What is very important , however, is that those decisions on the configuration and the
timing of the rebuild are matters for clinicians and health building designers not
politicians. I counsel Dr Clark, whose advocacy I admire —I have no problem with
that—against the political rh etoric around the rebuilding of that hospital, which, as I
know from experience, is a very, very complex process.
I want to defend and applaud this Government’s response to the support for the
Southern District Health Board. In the best of times, when the  so-called surpluses were
many and plentiful, Labour did nothing about Dunedin Hospital. It built a Chinese
garden but it cannot rebuild a hospital. The previous Minister of Health and current
spokesman on health in Labour has heavily criticised the fact t hat the windows in the
operating theatre are leaking. Well, I have got news for Mrs King. They have been
17 Jun 2015 General Debate 4493
doing that for years and she ignored it when Labour had an excellent opportunity. Then
when finances were tight and this Government had straitened time s, the commitment to
all of our district health boards and in particular the southern one was maintained. The
results are emphatic: a 30 percent increase in elective surgery throughput and reductions
in waiting times for cancer treatment and emergency department.
The worst part of Dunedin Hospital was the neonatal intensive care unit, which my
youngest daughter spent some time in after she was born. I cannot believe the patience
and good grace with which those workers spent years in terribly cramped and
overcrowded conditions. It was this Government that rebuilt the neonatal intensive care
unit, the children’s ward, and the acute mental health ward at Wakari Hospital. That is
commitment. That is making sure that health services are maintained in straitened times
and despite the financial challenges that the district health board faces.
I want to wish the very best for the commissioners, all three of whom I know very
well. Kathy Grant, Graham Crombie, and Richard Thomson have a mountain of work to
do and it is encouraging to me to know that the community is behind them and will wish
them all the best as they go on that path to viability. Yes, there are discussions about
population-based funding formulas and regional rural adjustors and things like that, but
the simple fact is, and we in the south should know this better than anybody —those
canny Scottish settlers have given that ethos of cutting our cloth to meet the need. We
fix those problems not by ignoring the financial constraints that are set for the
community. We live within those constraints and we make sure that we extract every
ounce of value from every dollar allocated to the Southern District Health Board. That
is the responsible thing to do, that is what the commissioners will do, and that is what I
wish them all the very best in achieving.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: Andrew Little is right. This Government
did start off with a bit of a hiss and a roar and then, as happens with many third -term
Governments, arrogant, out of touch, and out of touch with the community are the
themes that start creeping in. Is it not interesting that on the day that Nick Smith is out
on walkabout —out in never -never land or somewhere, out of the House , gone —the
Government sacks the Southern District Health Board? On the same day as the cheese
slides right off Nick Smith’s cracker —right off it: the same day. He is gone troppo:
gone bush. I will tell you this: if ever a Minister exhibited the themes of a rrogance and
being out of touch, it is that member Nick Smith.
What a litany, what a political catastrophe that man’s career has been. God alone
knows why the Prime Minister is so benevolent —in fact, a number of Prime
Ministers—as to put him back into Cabinet. Nick Smith is the man who in 1999 had his
first defamation case and lost. He is the man who in 2003—and, as I say again, that was
a time when the cheese did slip off the cracker; his headlights were on dim as he
wandered through life—lasted as deputy leader of the National Party for a long 21 days.
Then we hit 2005, the second defamation case—he lost again. Then in 2010 we find out
$270,000-odd of taxpayers’ money was spent on his legal defence. He then acquiesced
to and settled those two defamation cases. He had to make a payout and an apology.
Then we go forward, of course, to 2012: sacked from Cabinet for gross impropriety
in respect of ACC, and then he goes back into Cabinet as housing Minister. Then we
have a whole series, month after month, week after week, of the claim that there is no
housing crisis. Then in the Budget there was a rush of blood to the head. The lights went
from dim to high beam really quickly —maybe the fuse was blown—“We’ll come up
with a surplus land housing policy.” Yet again that was a complete debacle— I will not
waste the time by relitigating the excellent chronology that my leader went through to
evidence that fact —with the result, of course, that the iwi are now taking the
Government to court. What a litany!
4494 General Debate 17 Jun 2015
Then, of cour se, the ultimate irony, on a very serious note, was his response to the
death of an infant, Emma -Lita Bourne. I will read the quote because he denied it, you
will recall, in the House yesterday. He said on TV3’s The Paul Henry Show that “people
dying from pneumonia in winter was ‘not new’.” He also said: “People have got unwell
during winter, died from pneumonia and other illnesses for a very, very long time.” That
is what he said, and that is what he denied in the House yesterday —he denied it in the
House yesterday. That is an example not only of a Minister who is completely out of
touch—possibly with reality, definitely with the community —but of a Minister who is
so arrogant, so lacking in compassion that he would not even draw breath, breathe
through his nose, nod to the family, nod to the loved ones and express some sort of
remorse, some sort of compassion, some sort of sympathy. The best the Government
can do today after it has sacked the board—coincidentally when, yet again, Nick
Smith’s feet are firmly  in the fire —is to talk about that and not actually address the
issue. I just ask, in the high standards that the Prime Minister has for his Ministers—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Theoretically.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: —theoretically—what does this guy have to do to
get sacked, and what does the country have to do to be put out of its misery of putting
up with him? He has exhibited qualities of a person who should be nowhere near a
Cabinet door—nowhere near a dunny door outside Cabinet, let alone Cabinet itself.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: Closer than you, mate.

items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: If a person, Mr Bishop—and I suspect that member
would not be as stupid or dispassionate as Dr Smith, as he grins —cannot give a little bit
of compassion and acknowledge, as he is the responsible Minister, that perhaps his
department could have done better, that perhaps his department was indeed, as the
coroner said, partially, if not greatly, responsible as a contributing fac tor to that little
girl’s death, then there is something very, very wrong. The Prime Minister and this
Government should see Dr Smith for what he is: an example of where this Government
is going right off the rails, is completely arrogant, and is out of touch with the
community.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU -IIGA
items.text: It is an honour and
a privilege to speak in this general debate this afternoon. It follows from a morning that
I spent out in Porirua with thousands of other supporters of rugby, and supporters of
Jerry Collins and the Madill family, to celebrate a rugby legend—to celebrate a young
boy from Porirua who made good. We were there to celebrate certainly a gift from
Porirua to our nation, and that was Jerry Collins.
We all know that Jerry Collins was brutal, tough, and uncompromising on the rugby
field, but we also know that off the rugby field he was humble, he had a sense of fun, he
was loyal, and he was a family man. He represented this country with great ability and
achievement in 48 tests over his career.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: And a proud Samoan.

items.speaker: Hon Peseta SAM LOTU -IIGA
items.text: Yes, he was a proud Samoan too, Mr Macindoe.
The Pacific community revered him, upheld him, and uplifted this man, who did a lot,
particularly for young Pacific males to look up and dream and aspire to, just like Jerry
had done over those 34 years of his life.
La’auli Michael Jones, another legend, talked about him as being unique and as
being spontaneous. His sister Brenda spoke of Jerry, who had big heart, as we all know.
He had a lot of support, and our prayers and our thoughts continue to go out to Ayla, the
child of Alana and Jerry —both of whom, sadly, passed away 12 days ago— as she
recovers in a hospital in France.
We remember Jerry. We remember Alana. May I say to Jerry, ia manuia lau malaga.
Our thoughts, prayers, and sympathies go to his family and to her family.
17 Jun 2015 General Debate 4495
Today, as Jerry Collins demonstrated with his ability and his leadership on the rugby
paddock, the Hon Jonathan Coleman demonstrated his leadership in the health portfolio
by making the d ifficult decision to replace the board of the Southern District Health
Board and appoint a commissioner, Kathy Grant. She will take up that role in order to
bring this institution back in line and bring it back from the financial distress it is
currently under and to provide the quality health services that the people of Southland
and the people of the southern districts demand.
I was in Invercargill last week, and though I was dealing with matters around the
Department of Corrections, disability care, and ethnic communities, the subject of the
local district health board did come up. People were showing some concern about that,
and they have shown concern for a great period of time. Today’s decision, I think,
brings some of those concerns and those apprehe nsions to an end, and puts in place a
process and a team. Alongside Kathy Grant will be Graham Crombie and Richard
Thomson as deputies, and a third deputy with a strong clinical background is expected
to be announced later this month. That team will lead t he Southern District Health
Board back into the black, back into surplus, and back to delivering the quality services
that we expect —not just those people in the south but all New Zealanders. So today is
about taking over the improvement of that district health board.
Health is very important to New Zealanders. Health is one of those fundamental
portfolios, alongside education, law and order, and jobs, that New Zealanders demand
and expect from their Government. They expect services and they expect leaders hip,
and that is why, as an Associate Minister of Health, I welcome the decision that the Hon
Jonathan Coleman has made. It is an important decision to take a step forward, with this
district health board having taken several steps backwards over the years . So although it
is disappointing that the district health board failed in its duties, we are confident that
the commissioners who are going to take over the operations and the governance of this
district health board will do the job we expect them to do.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Tēnā koutou e te Whare. I just
want to start my speech in the general debate by acknowledging the passing of
economist and former secretary of the New Zealand Council of Trade Unions Peter
Conway. It was his funeral this morning, and I have just come back from it. Peter was a
kind, loving, and gentle man. He devoted his life to social justice. I think that he would
have actually appreciated and approved of the bill that I launched today. It is designed
to amend the Immigration Act to increase the refugee quota to 1,000 refugees, plus or
minus 5 percent. This bill has been lodged, and although I recognise that the refugee
quota can be raised currently by regulatio n, that requires the will of the Government,
and at this stage that will is missing. A member’s bill is the only means I have to
attempt to compel the Government into taking action on refugee quotas.
A former Prime Minister of this country with razor sharp  wit, David Lange, once
said that New Zealand was a country of insurmountable opportunity —basically, a place
where many of us have the opportunity to thrive. Interestingly, David Lange was the
Prime Minister the last time the refugee quota was raised, and that was in 1987—28
years ago. Since then, we have offered that opportunity to thrive to only 750 refugees
per year, despite the fact that in 28 years our population has increased by roughly 40
percent. Basically, over that period we have nearly halved the number of refugees we
take on a per capita basis. We take only 750 refugees from a total of over 50 million
refugees worldwide, and that is the largest number since the end of the Second World
War. Yes, it is a big problem. But, yes, we can do our fair share to support these people
who have been displaced, who have endured war, who have endured civil disruption,
and who have actually faced death many times over. These are the people who are
4496 General Debate 17 Jun 2015
desperately seeking a safe haven, a place to live —not just a refug ee camp, which is a
place to survive, but a place to live and a place simply to thrive.
There are people who would give the world to settle here in New Zealand, and many
of them actually do give everything they have. By taking so few refugees, we are fail ing
in our obligations as humanitarian global citizens. We are 88 th in the world in terms of
refugees per capita. Even Australia takes roughly five times more per capita then we do.
I do not think that we should think this is generous of Australia, given i ts appalling
treatment of asylum seekers in camps in Nauru and its appalling, inhumane, and illegal
treatment of people arriving by boat seeking asylum and basically paying off the people
smugglers. Before we think that Australia is generous by taking five  times our refugee
quota, we should look to the Scandinavian countries, which take 20 times more than we
do, and that is on a per capita basis.
Increasing the quota will cost—of course it will. Based on the information that I have
received from the Ministe r’s office, it would be about $19.2 million over 3 years, but
this is a tiny fraction of the Government’s budget. When we think about how much we
are spending on a referendum on a flag, I think we have actually got our priorities
wrong. More and more New Z ealanders want us to raise the quota. Organisations like
Amnesty International, the Red Cross, and the Refugee Council want us to double it.
Actually, even Newstalk ZB, with its poll, showed that the majority of New Zealanders
who answered the poll want to see the quota raised. This Government is out of touch
with ordinary New Zealanders, who want to take a compassionate approach to ensuring
that refugees can come to New Zealand. We can increase the quota. It is a life and death
situation for most of them, and we have it in our hands to make life better for them.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: If we needed an illustration of how
important good public services are for the lives of New Zealanders, then I think the
events around the Southern District Health Board’s non- performance over the past few
years absolutely illustrates and confirms this Government’s push and very strong focus
on providing good public services. Today’s letter by the Minister of Health, the Hon
Jonathan Coleman, to the Southern District Health Board, replacing it with
commissioners, is the circuit- breaker that we have been looking for and that we have
needed down south in the Southern District Health Board area.
I commend the M inister for his approach to this worrying situation, which has been
developing over the previous months and years. It has been particularly worrying not
only for the people of Dunedin and Invercargill but for the people of Central Otago and
also North Otag o. The reason for that is that the two rural hospitals, Dunstan Hospital
and Ōāmaru Hospital, have contracts for services with the district health board. If you
talk about the people of those areas, Ōāmaru is an area in North Otago with a fairly
static pop ulation, an ageing population, but we also have a number of new people
coming into our communities as a result of employment opportunities. Central Otago,
on the other hand, is an area of growth. It also has its fair share of older folk there with
their particular needs, but it is experiencing strong growth.
I met, many years ago now, a young woman who lived at Lake Hāwea. She was
pregnant and was concerned about her pregnancy because she was one of those to
whom it was signalled that she would probably ha ve to go to Dunedin for the birth of
her child. The implications of that were very stark. If one were to look at the Stuff
website, one would see that there is a bad weather and snow warning for all of Central
Otago and much of the south. What that would m ean is that if you were having a
planned birth at Dunedin Hospital, from Hāwea, you would almost have to set up the
day before. We are very remote down south. We are very remote from the base
hospitals of Dunedin and Invercargill, which is why it is so ver y important to maintain
the capability and the funding to both Dunstan and Ōāmaru hospitals. We are remote.
17 Jun 2015 General Debate 4497

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Her hospital’s underfunding. That’s why they are facing cuts.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: It is really disappointing when the Opposition members choose to
treat such a serious issue as an opportunity for political gain. Quite apart from the fact
that they are just wrong, the issues are very important to all of Dunedin, and I do hope
that that member chooses to take them a little more seriously in the future.
The rural health services review that was undertaken by the district health board over
the past couple of years promised to be an opportunity to provide better services for
those hospital s of Dunstan and Ōāmaru, but also Balclutha, of course, and Ranfurly.
The board promised to take a more modern view and more modern look at how we
provide health services for that woman living in Lake Hāwea, or for the person who is
experiencing a cardiac event in Wānaka or Ōāmaru and needs specialist health services.
It is entirely feasible these days for health services to be provided out at the rural
hospitals. If I can just reference the mobile health services —the surgical bus that travels
around New Zealand delivering day surgeries to patients at those hospitals, providing a
huge benefit in terms of convenience and cost, and with greater health outcomes,
because those patients do not have to travel. That is the future. That is the future of rural
health services.
I wish the commissioners—Kathy Grant, Graham Crombie, and Richard Thomson—
the very best in their endeavours because I would like to see this as an opportunity to
have another look not just at reducing the deficit, and not just at a better delivery of
health services to all people within the district health board area, but as an opportunity
to look at how we deliver health services better in the future.

items.speaker: JENNY SALESA
items.text: Talofa lava, Mr Assistant Speaker.
First of all, I would like to honour and acknowledge Jerry Collins, who had his funeral
in Porirua earlier on this morning. I and a number of Labour MPs were there to
celebrate his life. Manuia Iou Malaga Jerry.
This Government has failed to deliver on the brighter future that it promised us.
Seven years ago it promised us that it would deliver a Budget surplus; we have still not
seen that. It has lost its way, and it is stumbling from one disaster to another. It is now
dealing with incompetence—for instance, how it is dealing with the Tāmaki Collective
and Ngāti Whātua over Crown land in Auckland and how it is dealing with
Relationships Aotearoa. And one of my very own constituents, 2- year-old Emma-Lita
Bourne—may she rest in peace—died last year due in part to the incompetence of this
Government. There are many examples of where this Government has lost its way and
of where it fails to prioritise what is actually important—that is, New Zealand children
and their families.
This Government has spent $11 million on sheep for a businessman in Saudi Arabia.
It has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment signs, on a Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment rock, and,
we heard today, on a Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment desk. The
Government has wasted $26 million on the flag referendum, which a lot of people tell
us they do not really want. This Government has not even passed health and safety
legislation following the deaths of 29 New Zealanders at Pike River. Then there is the
housing crisis, which brings me to where I would like to focus today, which is on the
tragic death of 2-year-old Emma-Lita Bourne.
In his report, the coroner found that Emma -Lita Bourne’s death, in Ōtara, was partly
a result of the cold, damp, mouldy State house that she lived in. This is a damning
indictment on this Government. The State house did not even have any carpets. It was
not insulated. And the State departments that t he family dealt with were told many,
many times of the ill health that this toddler was suffering from, as well as that of one of
her siblings who was suffering from rheumatic fever. Mr English stated that Housing
4498 General Debate 17 Jun 2015
New Zealand insulates all of its propertie s where practicable. I think that the
Government needs to explain to the Bourne family the reasons why it was not
practicable to insulate the State house that the Bourne family lived in and why it was
not practicable to move the family. They asked many tim es to be moved from this State
house to another house that would have been fit for them to live in. Why was it not
practicable to move them until after the tragic death of this child?
I went door -knocking during the adjournment last week, including along t he
particular street in Ōtara where Emma -Lita Bourne lived. I tell you, it breaks my heart
to see some of these State houses and the conditions that some of these families are
living in still. Some of their houses are not insulated. It is actually colder i nside the
houses than outside the houses. I spoke with some of the neighbours who lived next to
Emma-Lita Bourne, who actually recalled seeing this toddler and how she used to play
on the streets and at the public park right next door to her house. Only a few days after
Emma-Lita Bourne’s death, we were also informed of another father of six who lived in
Papakura, and his death was also, according to the coroner’s report, because of the
incompetence of this Government and the condition of the State house that he lived in.
I would like, actually, to point to the quote from the Hon Nick Smith when he was
interviewed on TV3 on Paul Henry’s programme. Nick Smith is quoted, after the death
of Emma-Lita Bourne, as saying: “People dying from pneumonia in winter is not new.
People have got unwell during winter, died from pneumonia and other illnesses for a
very, very long time”. This is a very, very insensitive quote right after a death. The
tragic death of Ōtara’s Emma- Lita Bourne, as well as that of the father of s ix Mr Tovo,
is indeed the fault of this Government, and the Government has a moral obligation to do
everything that it can to stop its houses from contributing to the deaths of its tenants.
Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Just before I call the
member, I am going to ask the Hon Paula Bennett to speak just a little bit more quietly
when other members are speaking, especially about serious topics. Thank you.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: The Salvation Army’s report
into the state of the nation in 2008 expressed incredible disappointment that the
investment that was being made in social services and care for people was not
producing the result that it hoped. There are challenges that New Zealanders face and
that Governments face all the time, so laying everything at the feet of the Government is
an easy blame game to play. I would just suggest that  the previous speaker, Jenny
Salesa, go back and read that report from the Salvation Army regarding her Government
at that time and consider the words that were said.
What we need to understand is that during the most difficult of times that this nation
faced financially the health budget in this country continued to be increased year after
year. If you go back to 2012, and if you look at what was happening in, for example,
Ireland, it cut out $200 million of its health budget at a time when we increased ours by
3.4 percent. Ireland ended up with an $800 million deficit and many health
professionals lost their jobs. It was a time when we, as we have done year after year
after year, increased health spending, increased accessibility for elective surgery,
increased the number of doctors and nurses and midwives, and we have made it possible
for hard-to-staff places like rural Taranaki to have access to health professionals through
our bonding scheme. At a time when things were very tough around the world, out of all
of the 27 countries that the OECD measured, we were third- highest for health funding.
So the rhetoric we hear today does not have any data or facts behind it. It is political
bias and it is misinformation.
What we understand is that New Zealanders need to have confidence in whoever
governs their country. We have been returned for a third term, and that is not a
17 Jun 2015 General Debate 4499
statement of arrogance, as other people would say. It is just the fact that New
Zealanders have had confidence in this Government and, principally, it is because of the
gains that we have seen achieved over a number of years in the face of great challenge
and great difficulty. We have seen more children involved in early childhood education.
We have seen more people receive surgery. We have seen more doctors and nurses be
trained and be involved in the health profession. We have seen many, many
achievements, and that is why today the Minister of Health has decided to put
commissioners into the Southern District Health Board, because the gains th at we
expect for the benefit of New Zealanders and the taxpayer are not being seen in that
district health board.
Health budgets are under pressure all around the world and in this country. We in
Taranaki have had the tremendous advantage of having a new hospital built. From all
the accounts that I hear from people who have gone into that hospital for surgery and
appointments, the facility and design itself have facilitated a far higher ability to offer
health care and get more people to that place and receive the benefit of that hospital. All
of that is absolutely necessary, and if we want to see New Zealanders cared for in such a
way that we desire, then in order to have those efficiencies and those modern buildings
we have got to have strong financial ma nagement of this economy. By and large I think
that is what New Zealanders have seen in this Government. They are seeing the benefits
of prudence. They are seeing the benefits of discipline. They are seeing the benefits
when the Prime Minister made a whole  list of Better Public Services targets and the
work that we have done to achieve them. Thank you.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: You cannot have a healthy population unless you have a
healthy environment and the National Government’s hands-behind-its-back approach to
the logging and mining of swamp kauri in Northland is all about promoting an
unhealthy environment of extracting the maximum commercial advantage from nature
without any care about the consequences. It is really State-sponsored negligence by both
the Government and the Ministry for Primary Industries in allowing quite blatant
breaches of the Forests Act and the illegal export of these ancient kauri logs, which can
be tens of thousands of years old. Th e Forests Act 1949 was amended in 1993 after a
long campaign by the public to protect indigenous forests. It was amended to ensure
quite strict controls on the export of indigenous timber and timber products and there
are prohibitions in the Forests Act on  the export of indigenous timber unless it is in a
manufactured or finished form. Those controls were put in place to recognise that our
indigenous forests, whether they are standing trees or whether they are buried in
wetlands in Northland, are finite, that they are vulnerable to overexploitation if the
timber can be exported and a larger market created, and that they should be carefully
managed because of their value to Aotearoa New Zealand.
Some of these trees would have fallen at the end of the last Ic e Age. They have
remained buried in wetlands. Some of them are fairly intact because they are not
exposed to the air. They have got a value as taonga, as Dover Samuels and others have
called them, and, yet, under this Government the Ministry for Primary Industries is
turning a blind eye to the export of whole ancient kauri logs. That is because ancient
swamp kauri has a reputation as being one of the oldest timbers able to be worked in the
world and it has got a huge value in places like China, where it can sell for anything
between $2,000 and $10,000 a cubic metre. So what we have seen is a gold rush
mentality over the last decade because of these very high prices for the timber and that
has led to industrial -scale mining of the buried kauri forest in areas  around Dargaville,
Kaitāia, and throughout the north.
It is only in Northland that we get these buried kauri forests. They are finite yet the
Government is just closing its eyes to the plundering of wetlands and the plundering of
4500 General Debate 17 Jun 2015
these forests. Judith Collins says she does not care about wetlands. That is because her
husband’s company Oravida is too interested in taking the swamp kauri from these
wetlands. But wetlands have been hugely reduced in New Zealand. We are down to less
than 10 percent of their f ormer extent. We should be protecting our wetlands under the
Resource Management Act; not having local councils also being irresponsible and
allowing them to be dug up with huge bulldozers and earth-moving equipment.
It has been the work of citizens in Northland, and groups like the Northland
Environmental Protection Society, and the far north branch of Forest and Bird, which
has exposed the scandal that is going on here. They have sought numerous requests
under the Official Information Act and the work that the Northland Environmental
Protection Society has done shows that of the 53 notices of intention to export that were
filed with the Ministry for Primary Industries in 2013, 81 percent of those notices were
missing quite substantial information about th e milling statements and the source of the
timber. In the Forests Act there is an absolute prohibition on native timber being
sourced from indigenous forest land or dug up from wetlands and then being exported.
So it is really important that the Ministry for Primary Industries knows the source of the
swamp kauri, and yet when this information is missing from the notice of export
statements, how can it know that?
The Minister was saying earlier in the House that there is close monitoring, yet I
understand that the Ministry for Primary Industries often requires only a photograph of
the area to be logged or a map. It is not actually sending its staff out on-site to determine
where the kauri is coming from. And then we have this prohibition on the export of log s
and the export of anything over than finished or manufactured products. Yet what are
we finding? On websites like Alibaba there are a number of advertisements for logs.
What we are seeing is big planks of swamp kauri that are rough -sawn timber that have
had a brief bit of stain applied to them. Those are being exported as table tops. The
Ministry for Primary Industries needs to actually enforce the Act and prohibit these log
exports.

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: Thank you for the ability to
make a contribution to this general debate. I just want to make one remark before I start,
and that is for the Opposition members who wanted to have a snap debate on an issue as
important as the Minister of Health’s decision to put a commissioner into the Southern
District Health Board. The Opposition has not really made much of a mention of that
issue over the last hour or so, so I thought I would start off my contribution by just
clarifying a few points that were raised. Firstly, with regard to the Southern District
Health Board, I think I would like to congratulate the Minister on taking this decision. I
know it is about the third time in the past 3 decades a decision like this  has been taken.
It is not taken on a light basis. I think that it has been, from what I have heard from my
constituents, welcomed by the community, particularly the rural health centres—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: How about the cuts in the member’s electorate? Are they
welcomed?

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: Actually, while we are talking about cuts, the total funding to
the Southern District Health Board is at a level of about $852 million. There has been an
increase of $134 million over the last 7 y ears, including $15 million last year. There are
66 more doctors, 195 more nurses, and 2,557 more elective surgeries —a 30 percent
increase since 2008. So while we are talking about the data, it is looking pretty good
from this side.
But I would just like to reinforce the point that health is a sensitive topic and it is
something on top of the mind for everybody. I think that our community, certainly,
would like to reinforce the support behind the Government, and the Minister of Health
in particular, for ta king this step. I would like to offer my personal optimism for
17 Jun 2015 General Debate 4501
Southland and Otago and the confidence that I have on behalf of my electorate for
Kathy Grant and her team, and I look forward to working with her in the near future. It
is a project that she h as willingly taken on board that will not be a short -term fix, but
she is more than qualified, from all that I have heard of her expertise and background, to
lead this through.

items.speaker: Seguing into the purpose of my speech
items.text: the Better Public Services, which are a key
feature of this Government’s policies across the Public Service, are around actually
putting people at the centre of policies and at the centre of the outcomes of public
departments. That is actually a key feature of what the Minister of Health has done in
this decision that he has announced today, unlike the Labour Party, which was more
focused on making sure that Government departments kept getting more money each
year with no real delivery in outcome. An example I will use i s education. Over the 9
years when Labour was in Government it almost doubled spending on education with
no real gain in achievement. We have increased spending in education by about 45
percent. The achievement rates, right from early childhood education p articipation to
national standards participation to high school National Certificate of Educational
Achievement (NCEA) levels 1, 2, and 3, are going up and up each year. It is through the
remarkable contributions of Cabinet, and particularly Ministers working across the
social sector portfolios—

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: Hekia Parata.

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: The Hon Hekia Parata, the Hon Anne Tolley, the Hon Nikki
Kaye—these are real people who are looking across the Public Service and making a
strong contribution for real New Zealanders.
Just talking about the national standards data for NCEA level 2, in the latest data we
have seen we have had an increase from 85.7 percent to 86.8 percent over the last year.
Since 2010 we have seen NCEA level 2 participation rise by 7 percent.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: What about the TV screens? Where was Mr Bishop? Come on, fess
up. Play a continuous loop of him. He dropped the Minister in it.

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: It is interesting that Mr Clark over there is still talking about Mr
Bishop and not talking about the real issue at hand, which is actually the Southern
District Health Board and his constituents. I think if you would ask your constituents,
Mr Clark, about the Government’s need to put in a commissioner, they would be very
supportive of it, because they did not see those gains under Labour. They saw the
former Labour Government muddling around with health and no real gains.
This Government has increased elective surgeries and increased th e number of
doctors and the number of nurses —real, tangible gains across the board. So our rural
hospitals are in good heart. They are led by capable boards. They are led by capable
chief executives, passionate medical staff, and passionate volunteers, as well, across the
board, from our midwifery care right through to GPs and to other aspects of rural
hospitals. That is why they are united in support of the steps this Government is taking
to try to get some real results for the people of Southland and Otago. Again, I would just
like to reiterate my congratulations to the Minister on behalf of the people of Clutha -
Southland. Thank you.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

APPROPRIATION (2014/15 SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES) BILL
IMPREST SUPPLY (FIRST FOR 2015/16) BILL
Second Readings
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Associate Minister of Finance)  on behalf of the

items.speaker: Minister of Finance
items.text: I move, That the Appropriation (2014/15 Supplementary
Estimates) Bill and the Imprest Supply (First for 2015/16) Bill be now read a second
time. The Appropriation (2014/15 Supplementary Estimates) Bill relates to the financial
year about to end on 30 June 2015 and seeks parliamentary authority for variations to
appropriations authorised by the Appropriation (2014/15 Estimates) Act 2014 and for
new appropriations that were not in that Act. The Imprest Supply (First for 2015/16)
Bill relates to the new financial year starting on 1 July 201 5 and seeks parliamentary
authority, or supply, for Government expenditure during the first 2 months of that
financial year in advance of the passing of the Appropriation (2015/16 Estimates) Bill,
which was introduced, of course, on Budget day. On behalf of the Minister of Finance, I
thank the Finance and Expenditure Committee and the Intelligence and Security
Committee for their prompt consideration of these supplementary estimates.
Budget 2015 was delivered against a backdrop of sustained economic growth, rising
wages, more jobs, low inflation, and low interest rates. It focused on sticking to a plan
that is working: careful management of public spending going hand in hand with
investment in public services and support for the country’s most vulnerable. Budget
forecasts show an annual GDP growth of 2.8 percent on average over the next 4 years,
keeping New Zealand among the faster -growing developed economies. That growth is,
of course, working for New Zealanders. By mid- 2019 a further 150,000 people are
forecast to be in work and the average wage is expected to rise by $7,000, to $63,000 a
year. Unemployment is expected to drop below 5 percent in the next 2 years and then
fall further. Inflation and interest rates are expected to be significantly lower than
previously forecast. This is good news, of course, for consumers because their income
will go a bit further. But, as I have outlined previously, lower than expected inflation is
impacting the Government’s revenue.
The Budget forecasts a deficit of $684 mill ion for 2014-15, which is $2.2 billion less
than last year’s deficit. But my, are not things already changing? A surplus of $176
million is expected in 2015 -16, with increasing surpluses in following years. Of course,
you may have noticed that these are fo recasts with some degree of uncertainty around
them, and we saw this with the $448 million surplus in the 10 months to 30 April —
around a billion dollars better than forecast in the Budget.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Don’t get too excited.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Let me assure the member that I am not excited yet. The
surplus target has been successful in applying greater discipline to Government
spending, which has turned the Government’s books round, and the fiscal outlook
remains very positive.
17 Jun 2015 Appropriation (Estimates) Bill & Imprest Supply Debate 4503
What really matters is the overall trajectory of improvement. We have come a long
way from a deficit of $18.2 billion just 4 years ago, following the global financial crisis
and the Canterbury earthquakes. We are focused on ensuring that that trajectory
continues by delivering better public services, which will reduce vulnerable New
Zealanders’ long-term dependence on Government interventions. We have got 10 Better
Public Services results, and we are seeing improvements. There has been a 38 per cent
reduction in youth crime since 2011. The number of teenage sole parents on a benefit
has dropped by 40 percent since 2011, and immunisation rates for Māori are now almost
as high as for the rest of the population. Budget 2015 builds on that, with a $790 million
package to reduce hardship among children in New Zealand’s poorest families, and that
is the next step in the Government’s commitment to addressing the long -term drivers of
deprivation.
This package includes several important initiatives, such a s increased work
obligations for sole parents on a benefit, more childcare support for low -income
families, a $25 -a-week increase in benefit rates for families with children, and an
increase in Working for Families payments to low -income families not on a benefit.
That entire package really is targeting around 160,000 families —with 300,000
children—earning less than $36,350 a year. As in previous Budgets, we have been able
to spend a bit more on this because we are focused on reprioritising spending to
programmes that deliver results. We have continued to increase spending on health and
education, but with a growing focus on the effectiveness of programmes for those in
need.
I will not go through all the Budget initiatives here today, but I will highlight, o n
behalf of the Minister, a couple of other key programmes. Budget 2015 includes a $1.7
billion health package, taking the total annual health spend to $15.9 billion. This
includes $1.3 billion for district health boards, for extra services, cost pressures , and
population growth. The Budget also provides an additional $680 million for compulsory
education, taking the annual early childhood education and schools’ budget to $10.8
billion. Outside the child hardship package, the Budget also provides over $100 million
for further initiatives to support vulnerable children. This is a responsible Budget,
delivered by a responsible Government. New Zealand is well placed but there is more to
do. We will focus relentlessly on a strong economy and jobs, continue inves ting to
support families in need, manage spending and revenue responsibly, and increase
resilience to global risks. We will build on a plan that is already working.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Grant Robertson.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: That is right.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I nearly gave you an “Hon”.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: That is right, Mr Assistant Speaker. I have not changed
that much.
It was interesting that the Minister acting on behalf of Bill English could not quite
get through her statement about the G overnment’s surplus/deficit without a little
snigger. The truth is the new language fed to Government Ministers by Lynton Crosby
is to talk about trajectory. That is the answer. It is not about whether you are actually
going to get to a surplus or not. It is a little bit like Nick Smith’s conceptual house. It is
all about the trajectory that we are going on, despite the fact that as the Government
staggers towards the end of the financial year covered by the supplementary estimates it
staggers towards a failure, for the seventh time, to reach a surplus.
It is not about trajectory; it is actually about the integrity of this Government. Before
the last two elections this Government told New Zealanders that there would be a
surplus in 2014- 15. It may have been a legitimate debate for the Government to have
gone to New Zealanders before the 2014 election and say: “Do you know what? There
4504 Appropriation (Estimates) Bill & Imprest Supply Debate 17 Jun 2015
is a range of serious social issues facing this country that mean we can’t make surplus.”
The Government could have gone there . The Government could have gone there and
said: “We failed over the last few years to actually deal with child poverty. We failed to
invest enough in health to ensure that budgets are kept up and that people can get the
basic health services they want.” T he Government could have come to New Zealanders
and been honest and been up front and said that. But it did not. The Government went to
New Zealanders with its No. 1 economic priority being to be in surplus for 2014- 15.
That date was there; that promise was there. It had been there for two elections. That
promise has been breached.
Members on the other side of the House might think it is not important. They might
think they can just change the language and talk about trajectories and conceptual ideas,
but the reality on the ground is that they broke a promise to New Zealanders. They have
failed to reach that surplus.
As they do stagger towards the end of this financial year, the year in which they
promised New Zealanders there would be a surplus, they sit alongside an economic
record that the Reserve Bank Governor has now been clear is one that is struggling and
staggering along. There are members on the other side of the House who like to say,
perhaps when my back is turned, Jami -Lee Ross, that I talk the economy down. The
reality is that this is not me, Mr Ross. This is not me. This is the Reserve Bank
Governor coming along to New Zealanders and saying that there is no sign that exports
are going to recover. The Government, having outsourced housing policy to the Reserve
Bank, now outsources economic policy, and says: “Well, you had better sort this out as
well, because we haven’t got any ideas, as a National Government.” So Graeme

items.speaker: Wheeler has to be able to say
items.text: “Well, I will cut interest rates now. I’m wor ried about
whether that is going to pour petrol on the overheated housing market in Auckland, but
there is no sign of this Government stimulating the economy.” He has to act.
So this Government has failed to deliver to New Zealanders the kinds of benefits  that
would be expected from an economic growth rate of around 3 percent. In 2006—which
you might recall, Mr Assistant Speaker Mallard —the Government at that time had a
growth rate of around about 3.5 percent, and that delivered a multibillion- dollar surplus
and had unemployment as the second -lowest in the OECD. Fast forward to 2015: a
similar growth rate, but a deficit; 41,000 more people out of work than when National
came into office; a failure to lift exports; and a failure to invest in core areas like
education and health to the extent that is needed.
This kind of economic growth that the Government currently has is not delivering to
New Zealanders across the board. One of the reasons for that is that economic growth is
built on something very soft and very shaky, and that is the recovery from the
Canterbury rebuild. That recovery is important for the people of Canterbury, but it is not
an economic plan —it is not an economic plan. If we remove that from the growth
figures and then we take into account the high levels of migration, real growth per head
of population is under 2 percent now. That is why, right around New Zealand, people
are not feeling the benefits of this growth.
In the Northland by -election, and Mr Bishop is very familiar with this, the me ssage
that was given to the National Party was: “Don’t come up here and tell us we’ve never
had it so good. Don’t come up here and say: ‘There’s 3 percent growth. Isn’t it great?’.”

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Wasn’t it just: “Don’t come up here.” to Chris Bishop?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: That is right. For Chris Bishop it was just “Don’t come up
here.”, but it was a message to the National Party from the regions of New Zealand. It
does not matter whether you are in Dunedin or whether you are in Gisborne or whether
you are in Whanganui, what you will hear from New Zealanders in the regions is that
they are working hard but they feel like this Government has neglected them. You take
17 Jun 2015 Appropriation (Estimates) Bill & Imprest Supply Debate 4505
a look at the Budget, the imprest supply bill, and the suppleme ntary estimates and you
ask yourself: “Where in the investment in New Zealand’s regions? Where is the
investment in diversifying the economy away from our reliance on commodity prices?”.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: What about the wharf at Waitangi?

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: That is right. I will give Mr Finlayson credit for this: the
wharf at Waitangi. There is the plan to turbocharge the New Zealand economy from
Chris Finlayson. I understand Mr Finlayson has had a large print of himself put on the
wharf design so it will be there and people will see his beaming face on arrival at the
Waitangi wharf in the Chatham Islands. Good on Chris Finlayson for helping the very
hard-working MP Annette King achieve that long-held dream of the wharf at Waitangi.

items.speaker: Hon Christopher Finlayson
items.text: She did nothing.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: I will tell her you said that— I will tell her you said that.
But that is it. That is it in terms of regional economic dev elopment from this
Government and in this Budget. I will wait for one of the members on the other side of
the House to get up and say: “No, the regional research institutes are here.” Well, this
deserves a little bit of unpicking, does it not? The regional  research institutes —up to
$25 million. That “up to” phrase got left out when Steven Joyce made those
announcements during the Budget period. And also there are only three of them. So
only three regions in New Zealand are going to benefit, and I will bet y ou they already
know which regions those are. There are going to be a lot of disappointed regions in
New Zealand because that “up to $25 million” is not going to stretch very far.
That is the problem, because today we saw, for the seventh consecutive global dairy
auction, a drop in the global dairy prices. That is a 55 percent drop since February last
year and a 30 percent drop since March this year. To turn that into real numbers, that is
billions of dollars not present in regional New Zealand. It is toug h work for the farmers
concerned, and some of them have got very high debt levels and will have struggles
over the next 2 years, but it is also tough work for that wider rural community. Take a
small place like Ōpōtiki in the Eastern Bay of Plenty —$30 million will not be in that
community next year. In a small community like Ōpōtiki, $30 million makes a huge
difference.. That is jobs in the service sector. That is jobs in a community that struggles
without that.
That is what is missing from this Government— a long-term plan to say: “We can
grow the regions of New Zealand to deliver jobs.” We know there is huge pressure on
Auckland housing, and Nick Smith makes the problem only worse. He puts the pressure
on. But if we want and we expect people to go and live  in the regions of New Zealand,
there must be job opportunities there for them, and that will happen only when the
Government partners up with regional communities. There is no sign of that from this
Government. Instead, it is distracted by its own pet pri orities. Nothing is a bigger
symbol and emblem of that—and it is in the estimates here —than the flag. The flag
referendum—the $26 million flag referendum —says everything you want to know
about the priorities of this Government. A $28 million social bonds pilot for a project
that nobody knows whether it going to work—that is just a gross ideological
experiment. That is another $28 million. This Government has its priorities wrong.
If this Government were to introduce a Budget to this House that was about investing
in the future, supporting opportunities for future generations of New Zealanders, and
giving them the chance to actually own their own home, then we would be in there
supporting it, but that is not the Budget that has come to us. These supplementar y
estimates are the last gasp of the 2014 -15 financial year, which was a failure of a
financial year for this Government —a failure to reach surplus, a failure to grow jobs,
and a failure to invest in the regions, which now have another year of neglect from  this
4506 Appropriation (Estimates) Bill & Imprest Supply Debate 17 Jun 2015
Government. This bill will be opposed by the Labour Party because it is a continuation
of this Government’s failure to deliver to New Zealanders a sound economic plan.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: There is only one failure in this
House, and that is Grant Robertson. If the person who is the economic spokesperson for
the Labour Party cannot go 8 minutes without having to delve into the flag debate in
one of the biggest e conomic speeches of the year, that shows his competence around
economic management. That guy has no idea of what is going on in economics. He is
always going to be behind the eight ball on this.
But look at this. I have got news for the people of New Zeal and. I have got news for
the people of New Zealand that comes from the last election. I went on to the website
for the Labour Party. I know nobody does this, and I know I should not do it, but if you
go on to its election website and you have a look at it, it has on there a statement:
“Everything is paid for plus we’re in surplus.” Under the Labour Party everything in its
alternative Budget is paid for and it is surplus. So, under Labour, there would be a
surplus now. I want to know from the Labour Party wh at it would cut. Would it cut that
$25 to those beneficiary families, who had not had anything for 43 years? Is that what
the Labour Party meant when it said everything will be costed and in surplus? That was
the promise of the Labour Party at the last ele ction—that there would be a surplus.
There would be a surplus, no matter what. No matter what, there would be a surplus.
[Interruption] And we are talking about the appropriation bill, Mr Assistant Speaker, as
the last member did. Under that policy there would be a surplus.
The other line that is really important to look at is: “Labour will balance the budget
and run surpluses every year.” That is a direct quote from the Labour Party. I want to
know from the Labour Party what it would cut. Under the Budget  and under the
appropriation legislation, what would the Labour Party be cutting for hard- working
New Zealanders? What would it be cutting for beneficiaries? What would it be cutting
for the people who are going to benefit from this legislation today? I look forward to
hearing that from Labour, because it was telling us it would have been in surplus this
year. Every year it would be running a surplus. Every year there would be a surplus.
There would be no extra social spending under Labour.
The Labour Party goes out there and tells people that it is there for the people in most
need. Well, the people in most need would have got nothing under the Labour Party
Budget in the last month because it would have had to be getting a surplus of a large
amount. Under the National Government we actually went out there and delivered for
those people in need. We delivered for them.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Where’s the surplus?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Where is the surplus? It is coming. That surplus will  not be far
away.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am going to draw
the member’s attention to the bill— I think he knows which bill it is because he chaired
the select committee that dealt with  it—and ask him to at least occasionally make
passing reference to the supplementary estimates or the imprest supply legislation.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Yes, and for that legislation, it is very important that we look at
some of the funding that was talked about in it. The previous speaker spoke about that
in regard to regions and wanted to know what was happening in the regional areas.
Well, I say come to Hamilton. Come to Hamilton as a test of what that regional funding
is. Come to Hamilton and see a $2 billion expressway being built. Come to Hamilton
and see a $500 million redevelopment of a hospital. Come to Hamilton and see $100
million spent on new schools in my electorate. Come to Hamilton and see that we are
the first city to have broadband done across the city. Come to Hamilton and you will see
the investment in regional New Zealand that this bill is part of, and see that this
17 Jun 2015 Appropriation (Estimates) Bill & Imprest Supply Debate 4507
Government is delivering financial support for the regions. We have delivered for our
region. We have delivered the  strongest economic base for that city to grow and
prosper, unlike the Labour Party, whose members come into our city only at election
time, and when they do, they leave before 2 o’clock because they know that they have
got nothing to say. The people of our city understand that our Government, through bills
like this, has delivered the infrastructure that is needed for our city to grow.
When we hear from the Labour Party members, one of the other things they talk
about is moving away from primary industrie s. Well, I would like to see anybody in the
Labour Party who has actually milked a cow, who actually knows how to get their
hands dirty, and who actually knows how to do anything —especially Grant Robertson,
the member from Wellington Central. It would be l ovely to see whether he has actually
done any farm work and all that. It is pretty rich for Labour members to come in here
and tell us and the rest of New Zealand that we should be divesting away from the
industry that we are the most competitive in around the world. Our most competitive
advantage is in the dairy industry, and those members bag it day after day in this House.
They bag it day after day. That is not good for New Zealand, and it is not good for our
people going forward.
When we look at econom ic growth, it is interesting to have the New Zealand First
Party there, because the last speaker spoke about economic growth and said that if you
took away Christchurch and you took away immigration, economic growth would be
very small. Well, there are factors in creating economic growth. And I look over there at
the New Zealand First Party. Those members want to take away immigration. They
want to close New Zealand down, and go back to the 1950s. They do not want new
people coming to this country, and I say to the members on that side—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is now the
second strike for the member. The member will now address one of the two bills that
are being debated for the rest of his speech.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: When we look at the Appropriation (2014/15 Supplementary
Estimates) Bill—there were a number of comments made by the other side, and I am
just trying to deal with those comments—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: New Zealand First has not
spoken, Mr Bennett, so you cannot try—

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: No, but there were comments made by the other parties. The
Budget was delivered against that background of sustained economic growth, and that
economic growth is based on a number of factors. Many people have said that
immigration is one of those factors. Well, it is, and it is a good thing. We need
immigration. We need new people coming to New Zealand, and we need that for the
growth of this country, going forward.
When we look at it, unemployment is supposed to drop considerably in New Zealand
over the next few years. That is a direct result of the plan that is in this bill. When we
look at it, New Zealanders having good economic growth rates going forward is a result
of the economic plans that have been put forward. When we look at it, New Zealanders
are going to go into Budget surplus either this year or next year. It is a very short -term
difference between now and when it will be happening, but it will happen, and that is in
the best interests of New Zealanders, going forward.
With those surpluses, going forward, we have choices as a country and as a
community. Those choices are important because that is where you deliver the social
services that bills like this deliver, and that the Budget delivered for New Zealanders.
That is an important part of what we do in this House. We cannot put that at risk. We
cannot put that plan and that direction for New Z ealand at risk by making petty
promises and by trying to stop people coming into this country who will actually benefit
4508 Appropriation (Estimates) Bill & Imprest Supply Debate 17 Jun 2015
and build this country to be even stronger. It is very disappointing when other parties do
that.
When we look at it, this bill and the Budget itself included a lot of things out there
for hard -working New Zealand families. They included things for people in the
